name: decker
why: A HyperCard-style multimedia sketchpad with a scripting language revives an old-school authoring environment that few developers have touched.

brief.what_it_is: Decker is a multimedia authoring platform for making interactive documents that combine sound, images, hypertext, and scripted behavior. You paint, draw, record sound, and wire up navigation between cards, using widgets like buttons, fields, sliders, canvases, and grids, with optional scripting in Lil. Decks can be saved as a single self-contained .html file that runs in a browser (Web-Decker), or run in the native C application (Native-Decker) on MacOS, BSD, Linux, Haiku, and Windows. Lilt, the command-line Lil interpreter, can read, write, and execute decks headlessly.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage pitches Decker as a single holistic environment for digital arts and crafts, where you could write a zine, build an adventure game, make a utility, or doodle pixel art, and which erases the divide between users and authors. It presents HyperCard's index-card model as a key inspiration, alongside Bitsy, Twine, Flash, VisualBasic, and TiddlyWiki.
brief.how_it_works: A deck is a set of cards holding widgets, and every interactive behavior is built from those widgets. Scripts run in a sandbox that prevents low-level host access so Web-Decker and Native-Decker behave the same; an opt-in 'Danger Zone' exposes non-portable operations. Decks are stored in a line-oriented text format, which the README says works well with Git and SVN, and Lilt can manipulate them programmatically.

brief.install_notes: Homebrew installs the decker and lilt executables, but the GitHub README describes building from source: a C compiler and libc plus SDL2 and SDL2_image are needed for Native-Decker, and Nix users can run nix-shell. Lilt needs only libc. The README also gives an SDL1.2 fallback with reduced functionality, aimed at the OLPC XO-4 running Fedora 18 (sudo yum install SDL-devel SDL_image-devel), and says other platforms may need makefile tinkering. Web-Decker needs only a browser and the built HTML file. No accounts are required; the README does not describe first-run configuration. The homepage says binary releases for MacOS and Windows are on Itch.io, and that native builds from source include Lilt.
brief.standout: It is a HyperCard-style authoring tool whose output is a single self-contained HTML file that stays fully editable in the browser, and the same deck can be driven headlessly from a terminal by Lilt. It also has a deliberately small, creative-constraint design, with Lil described as a Q/APL-family language.
brief.status: Maintained, by the evidence I could see: the GitHub page shows 1,199 commits, about 1.6k stars, and 97 forks, and the homepage announces an upcoming Deck-Month jam in December 2026. I could not see a last-commit date or a latest release date in the fetched pages.
brief.caveats: Native-Decker needs SDL2 and SDL2_image, and the SDL1.2 build has reduced functionality. Scripts are sandboxed by default; the Danger Zone is opt-in via a DANGER_ZONE build flag or the endanger() function. The README asks that PRs avoid new features without a prior Issue, and it forbids material generated with generative AI. Bug reports need reproduction steps and the OS or browser. The license is MIT. The README does not say which features are missing from the SDL1.2 build. I did not fetch the Itch.io, docs, or trylil pages, so I can't speak to them.
quotes: Decker is a painting program. It's also a presentation tool, a database, and a game engine.
Decker is written by humans, for humans.
Decker is intended to be small, simple, and cozy. There are an infinite number of features that could potentially be added, but creative constraints are also valuable.
